steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper proposing compositional preference models (CPMs) for aligning language models. Explain the limitations of standard preference models used in RLHF, describe how CPMs work and why they help, summarize the experimental findings, and close with a contributions list.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Need for safe, interpretable LMs; RLHF and preference models
- Limitations of current PMs: overfitting/reward hacking; hard to interpret and oversee
- Our proposal: Compositional Preference Model (CPM)
- Advantages of CPMs
- Experimental findings
- Contributions

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Need for safe, interpretable LMs
  - LM capabilities advancing -> need safe and interpretable models
  - dominant alignment approach: RLHF (cite): train preference model (PM) on human judgments, finetune LM to maximize PM reward
- Limitations of current PMs
  - (1) overfitting the preference dataset; spurious correlations misrepresent preferences (cite)
  - heavy optimization against PM -> LM exploits flaws; reward hacking / Goodhart's law (cite)
  - remedy: inductive biases on PM or limit capacity
  - (2) hard to interpret/oversee; single scalar feature hides influencing factors
  - especially bad for complex preferences (helpfulness, harmlessness) = multidimensional attributes (cite)
  - as LMs improve, harder for unassisted humans to give feedback (cite)
  - remedy: another LM decomposes responses into simpler pieces evaluable by human or LM
- CPM
  - framework for learning a PM robust to overoptimization, transparent/interpretable supervision of complex behavior
  - decompose global preference into simpler questions = human-interpretable features
  - prompted LM (e.g. GPT-3.5) assigns numerical value to each feature
  - feature scores combined into scalar score with trained logistic regression classifier
- Advantages
  - (1) more robust to overfitting/reward hacking: pre-selected features = inductive bias bootstrapping preference learning; parameter space spanned by meaningful, robust features
  - (2) modular, human-interpretable supervision: hard question ("is this text preferable?") -> easier ones ("is this text easy to read?", "is this text informative?"), easier for LM to evaluate and human to inspect
  - simple instance of divide-and-conquer supervision (cite): recursively break down, then combine solutions (cite)
- Experimental findings
  - CPMs generalize better, less overoptimization
  - better at capturing human preferences
  - auto-evaluation with Claude (cite) approximating human evaluators (cite): best-of-n samples with CPMs consistently preferred over conventional PMs
- Contributions
  - CPM framework: robust, transparent; intuitive features + LLM as feature score extractor (Sec. 3)
  - evaluation: robustness (Sec. 4.2), generalization (Sec. 4.3), overoptimization (Sec. 4.4), preference alignment (Sec. 4.5)
  - intuitive explanation of optimization and responses (Sec. 4.6)

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
As language models (LMs) get more capable, there is a growing need for models that are safe and interpretable. The main approach to aligning LMs with human preferences is reinforcement learning from human feedback, which trains a preference model (PM) to predict human preference judgments and then finetunes an LM to maximize the reward that the PM gives. But the current PM methodology has some limitations. First, it can overfit the preference dataset. The PM can misrepresent human preferences by fitting to spurious correlations in its training data. If an LM is heavily optimized against a PM, the LM is incentivised to exploit those flaws. This is known as reward hacking or Goodhart's law. One way to deal with reward hacking is to put certain inductive biases on the PM or to limit its capacity. Second, PMs are often hard to interpret and to oversee. They project preferences onto one scalar feature, so it is hard to know which factors are influencing their decisions. This is a particular problem for complex preferences like helpfulness or harmlessness, which often include a multidimensional combination of attributes. Also, as LM capabilities get better, it will be harder and harder for unassisted humans to give feedback on the LM's responses. One way to deal with this is to use another LM to break those responses into simpler pieces that a human or an LM can evaluate.

In this paper we propose the Compositional Preference Model (CPM), a new framework for learning a PM that is robust to preference model overoptimization and allows more transparent and interpretable supervision of complex behavior. A CPM breaks one global preference assessment into a series of simpler questions that correspond to human-interpretable features. Then a prompted LM (e.g. GPT-3.5) is asked to give a numerical value for each feature. Finally the feature scores are combined into a scalar preference score by a trained logistic regression classifier.

- Advantages
  - (1) more robust to overfitting/reward hacking: pre-selected features = inductive bias; parameter space spanned by meaningful, robust features
  - (2) modular, interpretable supervision: hard question ("is this text preferable?") -> easier ones ("is this text easy to read?", "is this text informative?")
  - divide-and-conquer supervision (cite): break down recursively, combine solutions (cite)
- Experimental findings: better generalization, less overoptimization, better capture of preferences; Claude (cite) as proxy for human evaluators (cite): best-of- n with CPMs preferred
- Contributions: CPM framework (Sec. 3); evaluation on robustness, generalization, overoptimization, alignment (Sec. 4.2-4.5); intuitive explanation (Sec. 4.6)

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
As language models (LMs) get more capable, there is a growing need for models that are safe and interpretable. The main approach to aligning LMs with human preferences is reinforcement learning from human feedback, which trains a preference model (PM) to predict human preference judgments and then finetunes an LM to maximize the reward that the PM gives. But the current PM methodology has some limitations. First, it can overfit the preference dataset. The PM can misrepresent human preferences by fitting to spurious correlations in its training data. If an LM is heavily optimized against a PM, the LM is incentivised to exploit those flaws. This is known as reward hacking or Goodhart's law. One way to deal with reward hacking is to put certain inductive biases on the PM or to limit its capacity. Second, PMs are often hard to interpret and to oversee. They project preferences onto one scalar feature, so it is hard to know which factors are influencing their decisions. This is a particular problem for complex preferences like helpfulness or harmlessness, which often include a multidimensional combination of attributes. Also, as LM capabilities get better, it will be harder and harder for unassisted humans to give feedback on the LM's responses. One way to deal with this is to use another LM to break those responses into simpler pieces that a human or an LM can evaluate.

In this paper we propose the Compositional Preference Model (CPM), a new framework for learning a PM that is robust to preference model overoptimization and allows more transparent and interpretable supervision of complex behavior. A CPM breaks one global preference assessment into a series of simpler questions that correspond to human-interpretable features. Then a prompted LM (e.g. GPT-3.5) is asked to give a numerical value for each feature. Finally the feature scores are combined into a scalar preference score by a trained logistic regression classifier.

CPMs have several advantages compared to standard PMs. First, they are more robust to overfitting and reward hacking. The features that CPMs operate on are pre-selected, and this gives a useful inductive bias that bootstraps learning human preferences. This then limits how vulnerable they are to reward hacking, because the parameter space of the PM is spanned by features that were selected to be meaningful and robust. Second, CPMs allow modular and human-interpretable supervision of complex behavior. They break a hard question (e.g. "is this text preferable?") into a series of easier questions (e.g. "is this text easy to read?", "is this text informative?") that are easier for an LM to evaluate and easier for a human overseer to inspect. This is a simple instance of a divide-and-conquer supervision approach, which recursively breaks a problem down until it is easy to solve and then combines the solutions.

In our experiments, we show that CPMs generalize better and that using them leads to less preference model overoptimization. CPMs also perform better at capturing the underlying human preferences. In an auto-evaluation experiment where Claude is used as an approximation of human evaluators, best-of- n samples obtained with CPMs are consistently preferred over samples obtained with conventional PMs.

The contributions of the paper are:

- 1. Introducing CPM, a new framework for learning PMs that is more robust to overoptimization and allows more transparent supervision, by breaking the preference problem into a series of intuitive features linked to human preferences, and using an LLM as a feature score extractor (Sec. 3).

- 2. Investigating how CPMs perform on many dimensions, including model robustness (Sec. 4.2), generalization (Sec. 4.3), robustness to overoptimization (Sec. 4.4), and effectiveness for preference alignment (Sec. 4.5).

- 3. Enabling an intuitive explanation of model optimization and generated responses (Sec. 4.6).

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
As the capabilities of language models (LMs) continue to advance, there is a growing need for safe and interpretable models. The dominant approach to aligning LMs with human preferences, reinforcement learning from human feedback [1,2,3], consists in training a preference model (PM) to predict human preference judgments and then finetuning an LM to maximize the reward given by the PM. However, the current PM methodology has certain limitations. First, it is susceptible to overfitting the preference dataset. The PM can misrepresent human preferences by fitting to spurious correlations in its training data [4]. Heavily optimizing an LM against a PM incentivises the LM to exploit those flaws, an effect known as reward hacking or Goodhart's law [5]. One way of addressing reward hacking is to impose certain inductive biases on the PM or to limit its capacity. Second, PMs are often difficult to interpret and to oversee. They project preferences onto a single scalar feature, which makes it difficult to know what factors are influencing their decisions. This is especially problematic for complex preferences, such as helpfulness or harmlessness, which often encompass a multidimensional combination of attributes [2,6,7]. Further, as LM capabilities improve, it will become increasingly harder for unassisted humans to provide feedback on LM's responses [8,9]. One way of addressing this problem is to use another LM to decompose those responses into simpler pieces that can be evaluated either by a human or an LM.

In this paper, we propose the Compositional Preference Model (CPM), a novel framework for learning a PM that is robust to preference model overoptimization and allows for more transparent and interpretable supervision of complex behavior. A CPM decomposes one global preference assessment into a series of simpler questions corresponding to human-interpretable features. A prompted LM (e.g. GPT-3.5) is then asked to assign a numerical value to each feature. Finally, the feature scores are combined into a scalar preference score using a trained logistic regression classifier.

CPMs have several advantages over standard PMs. First, they are more robust to overfitting and reward hacking. The pre-selected features on which CPMs operate provide a useful inductive bias that bootstraps learning human preferences, which in turn limits their vulnerability to reward hacking, as the parameter space of a PM is spanned by features selected to be meaningful and robust. Second, CPMs allow for modular and human-interpretable supervision of complex behavior. They decompose a hard question (e.g. "is this text preferable?") into a series of easier questions (e.g. "is this text easy to read?", "is this text informative?") that are easier for an LM to evaluate and easier for a human overseer to inspect. This is a simple instance of a divide-and-conquer supervision approach [10], which recursively breaks down a problem until it is easily solvable and then combines the solutions [11,12,13].

In our experiments, we show that CPMs generalize better and that using them results in less preference model overoptimization. CPMs also show superior performance in capturing the underlying human preferences. In an auto-evaluation experiment with Claude [14] as an approximation of human evaluators [15,16,17,18], best-of- n samples obtained using CPMs are consistently preferred over samples obtained using conventional PMs.

Overall, the contributions of the paper include:

- 1. Introducing CPM, a novel framework for learning PMs that is more robust to overoptimization and allows for more transparent supervision, by decomposing the preference problem into a series of intuitive features linked to human preferences and employing an LLM as a feature score extractor (Sec. 3).

- 2. Investigating the performance of CPMs on a diverse array of dimensions, including model robustness (Sec. 4.2), generalization (Sec. 4.3), robustness to overoptimization (Sec. 4.4), and effectiveness for preference alignment (Sec. 4.5).

- 3. Enabling an intuitive explanation of model optimization and generated responses (Sec. 4.6).
